title: P*rn, Gambling, Genitals, and AI Slop: A Day in the Life of a School-Issued Laptop
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin, the Screen Time Consultant, compiles examples sent in by parents and educators of the inappropriate content children encounter on school-issued devices, and warns that the essay itself contains explicit language. She documents six patterns: reliance on YouTube for instruction despite filters, AI image tools inside Canva and Adobe producing sexualised results from innocent prompts, search bars returning disturbing results even for a single question mark, AI-enhanced Google search reaching children whose districts promised no AI access, gambling and consumer ads inside typing apps, and Gemini chatbot access appearing in Google Classroom. Her point is that schools do not vet these products before handing them to children and that filters and responsible-use policies give false assurance. She urges parents to test the devices themselves, share screenshots with the press and school boards, and treat district claims about online safety with skepticism.
points: Parents testing school-issued devices found sexual, gambling and AI-generated content reachable despite district filters and written assurances.
AI features added to existing ed-tech tools, such as image generators in Canva and Adobe and Gemini in Google Classroom, expose children to chatbots and images that nobody vetted.
Even a single question mark in a Chromebook search bar surfaced disturbing results, and districts treated it as a bug to patch rather than a systemic risk.
Typing and learning apps serve children video ads for gambling sites, soda and pharmaceuticals during lessons.
Cherkin recommends that parents test devices themselves, document and share what they find with local media and school boards, and be skeptical of vendor-driven claims about filtering.
quotes: Remember, sadly, that schools do not vet these products before handing them to children. They should, but they do not.
When the parent escalated to the district level, the IT department offered to block the link to the music video, “as though my child had not already viewed the video.

Even when districts assure parents their children do not have access to AI products, Google search has been so enshittified by AI that children are using AI, whether they (or parents or teachers or districts) realize it or not.
Typing apps come with video ads and pop-ups for gambling websites, which appear while children are supposed to be learning to type.
As these parents succinctly concluded in their email to their district’s leadership, “AI chatbots cannot do the work of protecting our children for us. That isn’t how or why they are built.

I am confident that all children have the opportunity to find content that is inappropriate, inaccurate, disturbing, or problematic, whether they seek it out intentionally or not (and most often, not).
Too often they are echoing tech-industry marketing propaganda, and they really have no idea what’s actually going on on the devices they have given to children.
